plan.topic: CagriSema (cagrilintide + semaglutide), the amylin + GLP-1 combination: how it works and what the REDEFINE trial program showed, including the REDEFINE 4 head-to-head against tirzepatide
plan.angle:
Hook (15 s or less): 'Did CagriSema beat tirzepatide? In the obesity head-to-head, no. In type 2 diabetes, the results were mixed.'

Then give REDEFINE 4 first: Novo Nordisk reported it as open-label, 809 adults with obesity, 84 weeks. Give both estimands, with each drug named next to its number: CagriSema 20.2% vs tirzepatide 15 mg 23.6% counting everyone, and 23.0% vs 25.5% if everyone stayed on treatment. Say it missed non-inferiority.

Add a short beat on the diabetes head-to-heads, credited to Novo Nordisk and dated:
- REIMAGINE 5 (Sep 2026): CagriSema 1.0/1.0 mg 12.4% vs tirzepatide 5 mg 9.1% at 60 weeks. Lower doses on both sides.
- REIMAGINE 4: non-inferior on weight vs tirzepatide 15 mg, but missed on HbA1c.

Keep the planned beats on amylin, REDEFINE 1 and 2, non-inferiority, open-label design and side effects.

Status line, re-checked on publish day: 'As of [date], CagriSema is investigational. Novo Nordisk filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in late 2026. A filing isn't approval.'

Close with: 'Don't switch or stop on your own; talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.'

plan.why:
Next-gen decoders are the only long-form format that travels for us (EloraTZP 373), and peer-reviewed NEJM trials make it verifiable in depth. The 09-28 Short only decoded a headline; this is the full deep-dive into the trial program. | fact-check: Good fit for the next-gen decoder lane, but the hook isn't accurate any more. 'In the only head-to-head obesity trial, no' leaves out two newer CagriSema vs tirzepatide trials in type 2 diabetes. In REIMAGINE 5 (Novo Nordisk press release, Sep 21, 2026), CagriSema 1.0/1.0 mg gave 12.4% weight loss vs 9.1% on tirzepatide 5 mg at week 60, which Novo calls superior. In REIMAGINE 4, as reported in secondary coverage, CagriSema 2.4/2.4 mg was non-inferior to tirzepatide 15 mg on weight but missed non-inferiority on HbA1c. Saying 'no' with no qualifier would mislead.

REDEFINE 4 as reported by Novo Nordisk: open-label, 809 adults with obesity, 84 weeks. If everyone stayed on treatment, CagriSema 2.4/2.4 mg gave 23.0% vs 25.5% on tirzepatide 15 mg. Counting everyone regardless of adherence, it was 20.2% vs 23.6%. It missed the 3.2-point non-inferiority margin. Under our craft rules, the narration and the screen must show the count-everyone figure next to the on-treatment one. Label these numbers 'Novo Nordisk reported' unless a peer-reviewed paper exists at script time.

Status: Novo Nordisk filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in Q4 2026. Secondary sources say it's still unapproved as of about Oct 12, 2026. A decision could land near the publish date, so re-check the FDA and Novo Nordisk on the day.

REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2 (NEJM 2025) are fine as planned. Copy the per-arm group sizes and the estimand from the papers.

Sources checked: Novo Nordisk REDEFINE 4 announcement via Investegate (https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/gnw/novo-nordisk-a-s-class-b--0qiu/novo-nordisk-a-s-cagrisema-demonstrated-23-/9442264); Drug Topics (https://www.drugtopics.com/view/cagrisema-did-not-meet-primary-end-point-of-noninferiority-to-tirzepatide); REIMAGINE 5 press release (https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/21/3365319/0/en/novo-s-cagrisema-delivers-superior-weight-loss-versus-tirzepatide-in-reimagine-5-trial.html, which returned 403, so I confirmed it through search results only); REIMAGINE 4 listing (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06221969).

package.description:
Did CagriSema beat tirzepatide? In obesity, no. In REDEFINE 4 (Novo Nordisk reported; 809 adults with obesity and a weight-related condition, 84 weeks), counting everyone: CagriSema 2.4 mg/2.4 mg 20.2% vs tirzepatide 15 mg 23.6% weight loss. In type 2 diabetes, results were mixed. Common side effects: gut-related, like nausea. As of Oct 18, 2026, CagriSema is investigational; FDA decision pending.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Don't switch or stop on your own; talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Did CagriSema Beat Tirzepatide (Zepbound)? What the Head-to-Head Trials Found
script.hook_pattern: Open loop via a direct question, answered within 10 seconds ("Did CagriSema beat tirzepatide? In the obesity head-to-head, no. In type 2 diabetes, the results were mixed."), followed by a 'both are true' paradox loop that pays off in the diabetes chapter

scenes.narration: Did CagriSema beat tirzepatide? In the obesity head-to-head, no. In type 2 diabetes, the results were mixed.

visual.stock_query: two medicine pen mascots in boxing ring

scenes.retention_device: Direct question answered within 10 seconds; 'mixed' teases a twist

scenes.narration: CagriSema is Novo Nordisk's two-in-one weekly shot: semaglutide, the medicine in Wegovy, plus an investigational amylin drug called cagrilintide.
Tirzepatide, from Lilly, sold as Zepbound for weight management, is the drug it had to catch.
In the next few minutes, you'll get the results from the key CagriSema trials, including every head-to-head with tirzepatide, with each drug named right next to its number.
And stay to the end, because one trial says CagriSema lost to tirzepatide and another says it won. Both are true. You'll see exactly why.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop: paradox paid off in 'The diabetes rematch'

scenes.narration: But first, you need to meet the hormone that makes CagriSema different.
Every time you eat, your pancreas releases insulin. But at the same time, it quietly releases a partner hormone called amylin.

visual.stock_query: friendly pancreas releasing two hormone buddies

scenes.narration: Amylin works like a brake on a meal. It slows how fast your stomach empties, helps hold back glucagon, a hormone that raises blood sugar, after eating, and signals fullness to your brain.

visual.stock_query: cartoon car brake on dinner plate

scenes.narration: Researchers have linked those fullness signals to a small area of the brainstem called the area postrema.
scenes.on_screen_text: A fullness hotspot in the brain

scenes.narration: That's a different pathway from GLP-1, the gut hormone semaglutide mimics. So the idea behind CagriSema is simple: pull two fullness levers at once.

visual.stock_query: two levers labelled amylin and GLP-1

scenes.narration: Amylin drugs aren't brand new. A short-acting version, pramlintide, was approved in the US back in 2005 for diabetes, and it had to be injected at mealtimes.
Cagrilintide is a long-acting amylin drug, given once a week. In CagriSema, it's paired with semaglutide in the same weekly treatment.
Tirzepatide takes a different route. It acts on two gut hormone receptors, GIP and GLP-1. So this is really a battle of two combinations.

visual.stock_query: two tag teams of hormone characters

scenes.narration: Amylin plus GLP-1, versus GIP plus GLP-1. Does stacking amylin on semaglutide actually add up? The first big trial gave a surprisingly clean answer.
scenes.retention_device: Question to viewer before chapter change

scenes.narration: REDEFINE 1 enrolled 3,417 adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. It ran 68 weeks and was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2025.
Here's the clever part of the design. It didn't just test CagriSema against placebo. It also tested each ingredient on its own.
2,108 people got CagriSema. 302 got semaglutide alone. 302 got cagrilintide alone. And 705 got placebo.
Counting everyone, whether or not they stayed on treatment, CagriSema led to an average loss of 20.4% of body weight at 68 weeks. Placebo: 3.0%.

visual.stat_label: CagriSema vs placebo, counting everyone, 68 weeks

scenes.narration: Semaglutide alone averaged 14.9%. Cagrilintide alone averaged 11.5%. Together, the average loss was bigger than with either drug on its own.
scenes.retention_device: Answers the 'does it add up' loop

scenes.narration: And here's an easy-to-miss detail. The trial let people stay on lower doses if they needed to. By the end, only about 57% of the CagriSema group were on the top dose.

visual.stat_label: CagriSema group on top dose at end

scenes.narration: Even so, the whole CagriSema group averaged over 20% counting everyone.

For context, tirzepatide's own placebo trial, SURMOUNT-1, in adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, gave 20.9% weight loss on the 15 milligram dose at 72 weeks counting everyone, versus 3.1% on placebo. That was 630 people on that dose and 643 on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Tempting comparison set up to be challenged

scenes.narration: But you can't line up 20.4% from one trial against 20.9% from another. Different people, different lengths, different rules. That's exactly why head-to-head trials matter.

visual.fact: Different trials can't be compared directly

scenes.narration: REDEFINE 2 asked a harder question. It enrolled 1,206 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, a group that has typically lost less weight in earlier trials of these medicines.
904 got CagriSema and 302 got placebo, for 68 weeks. Counting everyone, weight fell 13.7% on CagriSema, versus 3.4% on placebo.
Blood sugar improved too. 73.5% of the CagriSema group reached an HbA1c of 6.5% or lower, compared with 15.9% on placebo.
Impressive. But placebo is an easy opponent. The real test was always going to be tirzepatide.
That test was REDEFINE 4, which put CagriSema in the ring with tirzepatide 15 milligrams, the top dose of Zepbound.

visual.stock_query: two pen mascots face off in ring

scenes.narration: Novo Nordisk reported it as an open-label trial in 809 adults with obesity and at least one weight-related condition, lasting 84 weeks. Open-label means everyone knew which drug they were getting. Hold on to that.
scenes.retention_device: Planted loop: open-label design, paid off in 'Reading the fine print'

scenes.narration: CagriSema was given at its top dose, 2.4 milligrams of each drug. And Novo Nordisk reported two sets of numbers. You need both.
Counting everyone, whether or not they stayed on treatment: CagriSema 20.2%, tirzepatide 23.6% average weight loss.
If everyone had stayed on treatment: CagriSema 23.0%, tirzepatide 25.5%.

items: If all stayed on treatment: CagriSema 23.0% vs tirzepatide 25.5%

scenes.narration: Either way, tirzepatide's average was higher. And CagriSema missed the trial's main goal: showing it was non-inferior to tirzepatide.
These figures come from Novo Nordisk's own announcement, so the full trial details will add context.

visual.stock_query: press release paper with magnifying glass

scenes.narration: Now, 'missed non-inferiority' sounds like jargon. But it might be the most misunderstood phrase in this whole story.
Non-inferiority doesn't mean 'better'. It means 'not meaningfully worse'.
Before a trial like this starts, researchers set a margin: how far behind the new drug can fall and still count as roughly as good.

visual.stock_query: race track with dotted margin line

scenes.narration: Think of a race where the new runner only has to finish within a set distance of the champion. CagriSema finished further back than that.

visual.stock_query: two runners, one past dotted line

scenes.narration: So the trial couldn't show CagriSema was roughly as good as tirzepatide 15 milligrams for weight loss.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not shown 'as good' as tirzepatide 15 mg

scenes.narration: But here's the trap. Missing that goal doesn't mean CagriSema doesn't work. Counting everyone, it still averaged 20.2% weight loss in this trial. It just trailed tirzepatide.

visual.fact: It averaged 20.2% (counting everyone) but trailed tirzepatide's 23.6%

scenes.narration: Now, back to that open-label design. When people know which drug they're on, expectations can shape behavior: who sticks with it, who drops out, even how they eat.

visual.stock_query: person thinking with thought bubble pens

scenes.narration: Could that have nudged the gap? Possibly, in either direction. Nobody can say by how much, and it doesn't erase the result. It's a reason to read it carefully.
Then there are the two numbers. 'Counting everyone' includes people who stopped or skipped the drug. 'If everyone stayed on treatment' estimates the effect when it's taken as planned.

items: Counting everyone: closer to real life
If all stayed on treatment: closer to full potential

scenes.narration: Neither one is the fake number. The first is closer to real life. The second is closer to the drug's full potential. In REDEFINE 4, tirzepatide led on both.
So that's obesity. But remember, I promised you a trial where CagriSema won. Here it is.
Novo Nordisk has also tested CagriSema head-to-head against tirzepatide in adults with type 2 diabetes, in a trial program called REIMAGINE.

In September 2026, Novo Nordisk reported REIMAGINE 5, in adults with type 2 diabetes. If everyone had stayed on treatment, at 60 weeks CagriSema at 1.0 milligram of each drug gave 12.4% weight loss, and tirzepatide 5 milligrams gave 9.1%.

visual.stat_label: CagriSema 1.0/1.0 mg vs tirzepatide 5 mg, if all stayed on treatment, 60 weeks

scenes.narration: Novo Nordisk called that superior. That's the win.
But look closely at the doses. These were lower doses on both sides, not the top doses used in REDEFINE 4.
Then there's REIMAGINE 4, which used top doses in adults with type 2 diabetes: CagriSema at 2.4 milligrams of each drug, versus tirzepatide 15 milligrams.

In August 2026, Novo Nordisk reported that in this 68-week open-label trial, CagriSema was non-inferior to tirzepatide on weight loss, 15.2% versus 15.8% if everyone stayed on treatment, but missed non-inferiority on HbA1c, the measure of average blood sugar over roughly three months.
So here's the payoff. 'CagriSema lost' and 'CagriSema won' are both true. It depends on who was studied, which doses, and which outcome you measure.
At top doses in obesity, tirzepatide led. At lower doses in diabetes, CagriSema led on weight. At top doses in diabetes, the result was mixed.

items: Diabetes, lower doses: CagriSema led on weight
Diabetes, top doses: non-inferior on weight, missed on HbA1c

scenes.narration: And whichever drug wins on paper, there's another question that decides whether a medicine works for you: can you stay on it comfortably?
scenes.retention_device: New open loop into side effects

scenes.narration: Like other GLP-1 medicines, CagriSema's most common side effects were in the gut.
In REDEFINE 1, gastrointestinal side effects were reported by 79.6% of people on CagriSema, versus 39.9% on placebo.
In REDEFINE 2, in people with type 2 diabetes, it was 72.5% versus 34.7%.
Most often that meant nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation. In REDEFINE 1, these were mainly mild to moderate and tended to pass.
And notice that placebo figure. Nearly 4 in 10 people on placebo reported gut side effects too.
If you're ever on a GLP-1 medicine, your prescriber can suggest practical ways to ease nausea, like smaller meals, eating slowly, and stopping when you feel full.
So, can you actually get CagriSema today? Here's exactly where things stand.
scenes.retention_device: Question to viewer before chapter change

scenes.narration: As of October 18, 2026, CagriSema is investigational. It is not approved.
Novo Nordisk filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in late 2026. A filing isn't approval.

visual.fact: A filing isn't approval; decision expected late 2026

scenes.narration: A decision could come soon, so check the FDA or ask your prescriber for the latest. Until then, anything sold online under that name is not an approved medicine.
Meanwhile, tirzepatide as Zepbound and semaglutide as Wegovy are already FDA-approved for chronic weight management in eligible adults. Both commonly cause gut side effects too.

visual.stock_query: two pen mascots with approval badges

scenes.narration: Here's your cheat sheet.
One: in the obesity head-to-head, REDEFINE 4, tirzepatide 15 milligrams led CagriSema on both numbers Novo Nordisk reported.
Two: in type 2 diabetes, results were mixed. CagriSema beat tirzepatide 5 milligrams on weight in REIMAGINE 5. At top doses in REIMAGINE 4, it was non-inferior on weight but missed on HbA1c.

items: REIMAGINE 5 (if all stayed on treatment): CagriSema 12.4% vs tirzepatide 5 mg 9.1%
REIMAGINE 4: non-inferior on weight, missed on HbA1c

scenes.narration: Three: against placebo, CagriSema still produced large weight loss, 20.4% counting everyone in REDEFINE 1.
Four: whenever you see a headline, ask which dose, which people, and which number. Most headlines skip all three.
If you're curious about any of these medicines, bring questions to your appointment. Which option fits my health goals? What side effects should I expect? How will we handle them?
And whatever you're taking now, don't switch or stop on your own; talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The script passes, with four small wording and source fixes. I checked the main numbers against their sources and found nothing that would mislead a viewer.

- **REDEFINE 4 (obesity):** confirmed in the Novo Nordisk announcement of Feb 23, 2026 and in Drug Topics. It was open-label, with 809 adults over 84 weeks. CagriSema 2.4/2.4 mg was tested against tirzepatide 15 mg. Counting everyone: CagriSema 20.2% vs tirzepatide 23.6%. If everyone stayed on treatment: 23.0% vs 25.5%. Non-inferiority was not shown. Novo filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in late 2026.
- **REIMAGINE 5 (diabetes, lower doses):** confirmed in Pharmacy Times and the press release headlines. CagriSema 1.0/1.0 mg gave 12.4% vs 9.1% on tirzepatide 5 mg at 60 weeks, if everyone stayed on treatment. Novo called it "superior". It was announced Sep 21, 2026.
- **REIMAGINE 4 (diabetes, top doses):** confirmed in Novo's SEC filing (Form 6-K) of Aug 4, 2026. It was a 68-week, open-label trial. Weight loss was non-inferior: 15.2% vs 15.8%, if everyone stayed on treatment. HbA1c missed non-inferiority.
- **REDEFINE 1 and 2:** group sizes, the 20.4% vs 3.0% result, 13.7% vs 3.4%, and 73.5% vs 15.9% are confirmed by the ACC journal scan of the NEJM papers. The gut side-effect rates (79.6% vs 39.9%) match ACC's rounded 80% vs 40%. The single-drug arms (14.9% and 11.5%), the ~57% on the top dose, and 72.5% vs 34.7% match the NEJM paper as I recall it; I didn't re-open it.
- **SURMOUNT-1:** 20.9% vs 3.1%, with 630 on 15 mg and 643 on placebo. I didn't re-open this source either; the figures match the published trial.
- **Status and background:** an extended search on Oct 18, 2026 found no FDA decision yet, so "investigational" is correct. Pramlintide's 2005 approval and the amylin biology are standard and correct.

**Framing and safety:** framing is good. Each estimand is labelled, doses are named next to the numbers, the open-label point is honest, Novo's claims are credited to Novo, and the cross-trial comparison is correctly ruled out. Safety lines are present: the prescriber line, "don't switch or stop", and the warning about products sold online.

**Remaining fixes:** the GlobeNewswire link for s7 returned a 403 error, so I couldn't open it. There are also small wording and source-title issues, listed below.

issues.location: sources s7 (cited in sc01, sc05, sc47, sc48, sc52, sc53, sc68)
issues.problem: The URL returned HTTP 403 when fetched. A link that won't load breaks the rule against listing 403 pages. Its claims are confirmed by s7b (Pharmacy Times) and by press release headlines, so nothing in the script changes.
issues.fix: Remove s7 from the source list and from every source_ids array, leaving s7b. For example, sc47 source_ids becomes ["s7b"] and sc01 becomes ["s5","s7b","s8"].

issues.claim: Nearly 4 in 10 people reported stomach symptoms even without the active drug.
issues.problem: The source measured gastrointestinal adverse events. That covers the whole gut (for example diarrhea and constipation), not just 'stomach symptoms'. The wording narrows what was measured.
issues.fix: Narration: "And notice that placebo figure. Nearly 4 in 10 people on placebo reported gut side effects too."

issues.claim: Counting everyone: real-world view / Everyone on treatment: full-potential view
issues.problem: On screen, 'real-world view' is stronger than the narration, which says 'closer to real life'. Trial data aren't real-world data.
issues.fix: Items: ["Counting everyone: closer to real life", "If all stayed on treatment: closer to full potential"]

issues.problem: Both papers were published online first in June 2025, before the Aug 14 print issue. The source rules require labelling online-first and print dates.
issues.fix: Append to each title: "(published online June 22, 2025; print Aug 14, 2025)"
